nutshell: Unsupervised visible-infrared ReID (USL-VI-ReID) methods still implicitly assume every identity appears in both modalities during training (a 'paired' setting), which is itself an unrealistic, supervision-leaking assumption. This paper introduces the 'unpaired' USL-VI-ReID setting (some identities only exist in one modality) and proposes MCL, which synthesizes fake cross-modal positive features via a distribution-mapping module and aligns modalities at both cluster level (static) and instance level (dynamic).
contributions: Formally defines the unpaired USL-VI-ReID task and constructs the first public unpaired benchmarks by modifying SYSU-MM01 and RegDB - replacing a controllable fraction (α = 0.25 to 1.0) of visible-modality identities with images from external ReID datasets (Market-1501, MSMT17, LLCM) while keeping dataset size roughly constant.

Cross-modality Feature Mapping (CFM): a lightweight per-modality affine transform (learned scale/shift applied after normalizing by the target modality's estimated mean/variance) that projects a feature from its source modality into the target modality's distribution, treating the resulting 'fake' feature as sharing identity with its source - substituting for the missing real cross-modal positive pair.

Static-Dynamic Collaborative (SDC) learning: Static learning builds four cluster-level memory banks (real-IR, real-visible, fake-IR, fake-visible prototypes) and applies ClusterNCE contrastive losses across all four for coarse, mismatch-robust alignment; Dynamic learning adds an instance-level Cross-modality Label-Preserving (CLP) loss that pulls each real feature toward its own hardest-positive fake counterpart for fine-grained alignment.

New SOTA among unsupervised methods across all tested unpaired ratios (α = 0.25-1.0) on SYSU-MM01 and RegDB, and also SOTA among unsupervised methods (competitive with some supervised methods) under the standard fully-paired setting.
deficiencies: The 'unpaired' benchmark is constructed by literally swapping in images from unrelated external ReID datasets (Market-1501/MSMT17/LLCM) for a fraction of visible identities - so part of what the model learns to handle is cross-dataset domain shift for the swapped identities, not necessarily the same character of unpairing that would arise from, e.g., a person simply never being captured by both camera types within one consistent surveillance deployment.

CFM's core mechanism is a single global affine transform per modality matching only first-order/second-order statistics (mean and variance) - essentially an AdaIN-style operation. The paper never measures how faithful or identity-preserving the resulting 'fake' features actually are (e.g., nearest-neighbor identity accuracy of mapped features) - only downstream ReID accuracy is reported, so it's unclear how much of the gain is genuine cross-modal identity transfer versus general regularization from extra training signal.

The paper's own ablation (Table 3) shows Static Learning alone contributes more than Dynamic Learning alone (+5.19 vs +3.38 mAP on SYSU-MM01 All Search over baseline), and combining both (54.29% mAP) lands close to what adding the two individual gains would predict - the 'collaborative' framing implies synergy, but the ablation doesn't clearly demonstrate interaction beyond roughly additive combination.

Performance degrades sharply as the unpaired ratio increases - SYSU-MM01 All-Search mAP drops from 57.74 at α=0.25 to 44.95 at α=1.0 (~13 points) - and the paper's own Limitations section concedes MCL 'still faces challenges in extremely unpaired settings,' which is arguably the more realistic real-world case the paper is motivated by.
notable: Figure 3's t-SNE and similarity-distribution visualization honestly shows that even with MCL, 'some same-identity samples remain dispersed' under unpaired settings - a comparatively rare instance in this literature batch of a paper using its own qualitative figure to acknowledge an unsolved problem rather than only showcase clean success, worth noting as a model of transparent reporting.
